'''''Casuarina cunninghamiana''''', commonly known as '''river oak''', '''river sheoak'''<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Casuarina~cunninghamiana |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref> or '''creek oak''',<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|pages=80–81|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&q=%22Casuarina+cristata%22&pg=PA78}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Casuarinaceae]] and is native to Australia and New Guinea. It is a tree with fissured and scaly bark, sometimes drooping branchlets, the leaves reduced to scales in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of 6 to 10, the fruit {{cvt|7–14|mm}} long containing winged seeds ([[samara (fruit)|samaras]]) {{cvt|3–4|mm}} long.

==Description==
''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' is a [[Dioecy|dioecious]] tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|15–35|m}}, has a 
[[diameter at breast height|DBH]] of {{cvt|0.5–1.5|m}}. Its bark is finely fissured, scaly and greyish brown. The branchlets are often drooping, {{cvt|100–250|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to scale-like teeth {{cvt|0.3–0.5|mm|sigfig=1}} long, arranged in whorls of 6 to 10 around the branchlets. The sections of branchlet between the leaf whorls (the "articles") are {{cvt|4–9|mm|sigfig=1}} long and {{cvt|0.4–0.7|mm|sigfig=1}} wide. The flowers on male trees are arranged in spikes {{cvt|4–40|mm|1}} long, the [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] {{cvt|0.4–0.7|mm|sigfig=1}} long. The female cones are on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2–9|mm|sigfig=1}} long and sparsely covered with soft hairs. Mature cones are usually {{cvt|7–14|mm|sigfig=1}} long and {{cvt|4–6|mm|sigfig=2}} in diameter, the samaras {{cvt|3–4|mm}} long.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20cunninghamiana |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' was first formally described in 1848 by [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel|Friedrich Miquel]] in his book ''Revisio critica Casuarinarum'' from specimens collected by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]] near [[Moreton Bay]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/458022|publisher=APNI|access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''cunninghamiana'') honours the collector of the [[Type (biology)|type]] specimens.<ref name="Boland" />

In 1989, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] and [[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]] described subsp. ''miodon'' in the ''[[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]]'', and the name, and that of the [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:

*''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' <small>Miq.</small> subsp. ''cunninghamiana''<ref name="APC1">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''cunninghamiana''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55764 |publisher=Australian Plant Census |access-date= 27 April 2023}}</ref> is a tree to {{cvt|15–35|m}}, the articles {{cvt|6–9|mm}} long with 8 to 10 teeth.<ref name="RBGS1">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''cunninghamiana'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=in&name=Casuarina~cunninghamiana~subsp.+cunninghamiana |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref><ref name="foa1">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''cunninghamiana'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20cunninghamiana%20subsp.%20cunninghamiana |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref>
*''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''miodon'' <small>L.A.S.Johnson</small><ref name="APC2">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''miodon'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/55768 |publisher=Australian Plant Census |access-date= 27 April 2023}}</ref> is a tree to {{cvt|20|m}}, the articles {{cvt|4–7|mm}} long with 6 or 7 teeth.<ref name="foa2">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''miodon'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20cunninghamiana%20subsp.%20miodon |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This casuarina mainly grows in pure stands in open forest on the banks of freshwater rivers and streams in Australia and New Guinea.<ref name="Boland" /><ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:159845-1 |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref><ref name=dopi>{{cite web|last1=Boxshall|first1=Ben|last2=Jenkyn|first2=Tim|title=River she-oak|url=http://new.dpi.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/1918/river_she-oak.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090915121924/http://new.dpi.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/1918/river_she-oak.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=15 September 2009|work=Department of Primary Industries|publisher=Victorian Government|access-date=23 April 2011}}</ref>

Subspecies ''cunninghamiana'' occurs from [[Laura, Queensland|Laura]], [[Chillagoe]] and [[Augathella]] in Queensland to [[Condobolin]] and [[Narrandera]] in New South Wales, and the [[Australian Capital Territory]].<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland" /><ref name="foa1" /> Subspecies ''miodon'' occurs between the [[Daly River (Northern Territory)|Daly River]] in the north of the Northern Territory to the [[Gulf of Carpentaria]] in Queensland.<ref name="foa2" /><ref name="NT">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''miodon'' |url=http://eflora.nt.gov.au/factsheet?id=1088 |publisher=Northern Territory Government |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref>

==Uses==
River oak is widely recognised as an important tree for stabilising riverbanks and for soil erosion prevention accepting wet and dry soils. The foliage is quite palatable to stock.<ref name="Boland" />

==Invasive species==
''Casuarina cunninghamiana'' is an [[invasive species]] in the [[Everglades]] in [[Florida]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Biological control of Australian native Casuarina species in the USA |url=http://www.csiro.au/science/ps334.html |work=Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation |access-date=16 September 2010 |date=16 May 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605113952/http://www.csiro.au/science/ps334.html |archive-date=5 June 2011 }}</ref> and in South Africa.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.plantzafrica.co.za/miscell/aliens3.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006154123/http://www.plantzafrica.co.za/miscell/aliens3.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 October 2014|title=SANBI:Declared Weeds & Invader Plants|publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute|access-date=25 September 2014}}</ref>
